clinicalPearls: Amenorrhea is the absence of menses: primary when bleeding has never occurred without hormonal treatment, secondary when established cycles stop for 3-6 months; primary amenorrhea is rare (<1% of women), whereas roughly 3-5% of women have at least 3 months of secondary amenorrhea in a given year.
Pregnancy is the single most common cause of amenorrhea and must be excluded in every case with a beta-hCG, regardless of the history offered.

A normal cycle recurs every 21-35 days, lasts 4-7 days, and involves up to about 80 mL of blood loss; the term abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) has replaced dysfunctional uterine bleeding and is categorized by the PALM-COEIN scheme (structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy/hyperplasia; non-structural: coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not yet classified).
Evaluation of ovulatory disorders rests on three initial tests: a pregnancy test, an FSH level (to localize the problem to the ovary versus a central cause), and assessment for hyperandrogenism.

FSH is a better marker of ovarian failure than LH because it reflects loss of negative feedback from both estradiol and the inhibins and is less variable; anti-mullerian hormone (AMH) is also low in primary ovarian insufficiency.

Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is a diagnosis of exclusion, typically driven by a mismatch between energy expenditure and intake and/or significant stress, with suppressed GnRH, low gonadotropins, and normal prolactin; eating disorders, excessive exercise, and chronic disease must be specifically ruled out.
Isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH) is three times more common in men; about half of affected women have anosmia (Kallmann syndrome), and roughly half have an identifiable genetic cause.

Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) - the preferred term over premature menopause/ovarian failure - denotes ovarian failure before age 40, accounts for about 10% of secondary amenorrhea, and can wax and wane so serial measurements may be needed.
Roughly up to one-third of women between menarche and menopause experience abnormal uterine bleeding at some point.

Up to 60% of pelvic pain is attributable to gastrointestinal causes (appendicitis, cholecystitis, infection, obstruction, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease); urinary and musculoskeletal disorders are also common, so pelvic pain is frequently not gynecologic in origin.

Beta-hCG normally roughly doubles every 48 h in the early first trimester, and 99% of viable intrauterine pregnancies show at least a 53% rise over 2 days; the discriminatory zone (about 1500-3000 IU/mL) is the level above which a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on ultrasound.

Dysmenorrhea begins with menstrual flow and eases over 12-72 h; primary dysmenorrhea is largely prostaglandin-mediated, while secondary dysmenorrhea reflects underlying pelvic pathology such as endometriosis or adenomyosis.
harrison.pathophysiology: Menstrual function depends on coordinated signaling among four compartments - hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, and uterus/outflow tract - linked by feedback loops involving GnRH, the gonadotropins FSH and LH, and the ovarian products estradiol, progesterone, and the inhibins (inhibin A and B). Disorders divide into outflow-tract/uterine problems and ovulatory disorders. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism arises when anatomic, genetic, or functional disturbances impair hypothalamic GnRH output or pituitary responsiveness, producing low estrogen with normal or low LH/FSH; in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, energy deficit and stress raise CRH, suppress GnRH, and lower TRH input, with leptin and hypothalamic kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin signaling transducing metabolic and stress cues to the GnRH pulse generator. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (ovarian insufficiency) removes negative feedback, raising FSH and LH. In PCOS, abnormal GnRH pulsatility elevates LH and drives ovarian androgen output, and insulin resistance in muscle and fat further augments insulin-stimulated ovarian androgen production; frequent anovulation yields irregular menses and unopposed estrogen effect on the endometrium. Pelvic pain shares mechanisms with abdominal pain - parietal peritoneal inflammation, hollow-viscus obstruction, vascular compromise (e.g., ovarian torsion), and abdominal-wall pain - and may be referred from extrapelvic sources. Primary dysmenorrhea is mediated chiefly by prostaglandin pathways causing intense uterine contractions, reduced blood flow, and peripheral nerve hypersensitivity, with PG-independent mediators such as platelet-activating factor also contributing. Endometriosis reflects ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus that respond to hormonal stimulation.
additionalDifferentials: Pregnancy (must be excluded first in amenorrhea and in any reproductive-age woman with pelvic pain or bleeding)
Outflow-tract obstruction: transverse vaginal septum, imperforate hymen
Androgen insensitivity syndrome (about 10% of primary amenorrhea; 46,XY karyotype, female external genitalia, absent pubic/axillary hair, male-range testosterone)
Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions, usually post-curettage; genital tuberculosis in endemic areas)
Hypothalamic/pituitary tumors and infiltrative disease, hyperprolactinemia, Sheehan's syndrome, lymphocytic hypophysitis, prior cranial irradiation
Primary ovarian insufficiency (idiopathic, Turner syndrome, autoimmune polyglandular failure, fragile X premutation, post-chemo/radiotherapy)
Rarer causes of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: FSH/LH receptor mutations, aromatase deficiency, 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency
Pelvic pain mimics outside the reproductive tract: appendicitis, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, urinary tract disorders, musculoskeletal/neuromuscular and psychosomatic causes
infectionMimics: Pelvic inflammatory disease (upper genital tract infection, often Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae)
Tuberculous salpingitis / genital tuberculosis (also a cause of Asherman's syndrome in endemic regions)
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis complicating PID, presenting with right upper quadrant pain)
nonInfectiousMimics: Uterine fibroids (including acutely degenerating leiomyoma) and adenomyosis
additionalInvestigations: Beta-hCG to exclude pregnancy in every amenorrhea and acute pelvic pain evaluation
FSH (and LH) to localize ovulatory failure to ovary versus central cause; serial/repeat sampling in suspected POI
Prolactin in all patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Estradiol, testosterone and androgen assessment for hyperandrogenism; AMH (low in POI, may be elevated in PCOS)
Karyotype in primary amenorrhea with suspected chromosomal cause and in all POI patients

POI work-up: anti-cortical and 21-hydroxylase antibodies (specific but not sensitive for future adrenal insufficiency), thyroid function and thyroid peroxidase antibodies, FMR1 premutation screening, and bone mineral density (ovarian biopsy is NOT indicated)
Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal) as first-line imaging for amenorrhea work-up, pelvic pain, ovarian cysts, torsion (with Doppler for ovarian blood flow), endometrioma, and fibroids
MRI of the pelvis for better delineation of reproductive-tract anomalies before surgery and for higher sensitivity/specificity in endometriosis
Cranial MRI when history is atypical, with headache, other hypothalamic dysfunction, or hyperprolactinemia
Wet-mount of vaginal discharge plus nucleic acid amplification testing for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae in suspected PID
CA-125 may be elevated in endometriosis but has low negative predictive value; diagnostic laparoscopy is the gold standard for endometriosis when empiric treatment fails
redFlags: Shock or peritoneal signs in a woman with pelvic pain - identify life-threatening conditions first as they may need emergent surgery
Reproductive-age woman with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding - maintain high suspicion for ectopic pregnancy regardless of contraceptive use; tubal rupture is a life-threatening emergency
Severe pain with fever and peritoneal signs in PID suggests tubo-ovarian abscess or peritonitis
Right upper quadrant pain in PID suggests perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome)
Acute unilateral intermittent pain raising concern for ovarian torsion (confirm by absent Doppler flow)
Atypical amenorrhea history with headache, signs of hypothalamic dysfunction, short stature, diabetes insipidus, or galactorrhea - evaluate for a neuroanatomic lesion
Heavy or prolonged bleeding warrants prompt attention, but infrequent or absent bleeding is often under-reported and should be actively elicited
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends on cause. Many causes of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea are reversible with restoration of energy balance, though bone density may not fully recover with hormone replacement alone. Amenorrhea of any cause is usually associated with chronically low estrogen, carrying risk to bone and cardiovascular health if untreated. PID untreated risks infertility and ectopic pregnancy, and subclinical PID remains a major worldwide cause of these complications. PCOS carries elevated long-term risk of metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, steatotic liver disease, and a two- to sixfold increase in endometrial hyperplasia/cancer from chronic anovulation; symptoms often improve with age, with most women regaining regular menses and normal androgens by the fourth decade. POI is associated with additional health problems and infertility, though oocyte donation has high success. Ectopic pregnancy with tubal rupture can be fatal.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude pregnancy before pursuing an amenorrhea or pelvic-pain work-up.
Overlooking infrequent or absent menses because the patient does not volunteer it - a focused menstrual history is needed at every encounter.
Attributing pelvic pain to the reproductive tract when up to 60% of cases are gastrointestinal and urinary/musculoskeletal causes are common.
Waiting for positive microbiology before treating suspected PID - a presumptive clinical diagnosis is sufficient to begin treatment, and negative tests do not exclude it.
Confusing androgen insensitivity syndrome with mullerian agenesis - absent pubic/axillary hair and a male-range testosterone distinguish AIS.

Diagnosing PCOS without excluding mimics (hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia, adrenal hyperandrogenism); it is a diagnosis of exclusion, and in adolescents one should wait at least 3 years after menarche and not rely on ultrasound/AMH criteria.
Performing ovarian biopsy in POI - it is not indicated; routine genetic testing beyond FMR1 is also not currently recommended.
Assuming endometriosis severity at laparoscopy correlates with pain - it does not always; a normal CA-125 does not exclude endometriosis.
Delaying surgery for outflow-tract obstruction - early correction reduces the risk of endometriosis from retrograde menstruation.
harrison.severityClassification: Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized etiologically by the PALM-COEIN system (structural causes: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia; non-structural: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). PCOS is diagnosed by the updated Rotterdam criteria (2023 international guidelines): two of three among irregular menses (fewer than 8 per year), clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (>=20 antral follicles or ovarian volume >=10 cm3 in one ovary) or elevated AMH, yielding hyperandrogenic and non-hyperandrogenic phenotypes. Pelvic pain is classified as acute versus chronic and cyclic versus noncyclic to guide evaluation. Endometriosis is staged by laparoscopy.
management: Exclude pregnancy with beta-hCG and direct treatment at the underlying cause identified through the PALM-COEIN framework
Restore energy balance and address disordered eating or excessive exercise in functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea, with oestrogen replacement to protect bone
Medical management of heavy or abnormal uterine bleeding with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, combined hormonal contraception, progestogens, tranexamic acid or NSAIDs
Surgical treatment of structural lesions such as polypectomy or myomectomy where indicated
Hormone replacement therapy until the usual age of menopause in primary ovarian insufficiency, with fertility and oocyte-donation counselling
Dopamine agonist therapy for hyperprolactinaemic amenorrhoea
Bone mineral density surveillance in sustained hypo-oestrogenism, with gynaecology and reproductive endocrinology input and psychological support
